source.title: Evaluating Defences against Unsafe Feedback in RLHF
source.authors: Domenic Rosati; Giles Edkins; Harsh Raj; David Atanasov; Subhabrata Majumdar; Janarthanan Rajendran; Frank Rudzicz; Hassan Sajjad

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present. Some figure content is flattened, so Figure 2 does not provide reliably assignable numeric values.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether harmful supervised fine-tuning can make a safety-aligned model produce harmful answers, using the paper's own SFT attacks and harmfulness measure. Its main focus, however, is reverse-preference attacks and defences in RLHF.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work on harmful fine-tuning and shallow safety, but cited findings are not recorded as results here. Figure 2 reports SFT curves, but does not provide reliably readable per-ratio values in the supplied text. Results about defences are included where the paper reports harmfulness after an SFT attack; other metrics such as helpfulness, perplexity, KL, and reward are not rows for V1.
record.test_reason: The study trains safety-aligned llama2-7b-chat on 1,000 harmful samples, using SFT and reverse-preference DPO/PPO. Harmfulness rises from 0.06–0.07 to 0.59–0.83 (Table 1). This bears directly on V1, and the RLHF/preference setting is new. Most of the paper evaluates defences, which is mitigation rather than a test of V1 on a standard safety-trained model.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but needs correcting. The authors conclude that safety-aligned LLMs are easily made harmful by reverse-preference attacks (DPO/PPO), as effective as or more than SFT, though SFT is easier to perform. Online defences (Refusal Loss, Lisa) are generally protective but need very high loss weights. Offline defences are generally ineffective, and no defence is fully reliable. Some defences 'harmlessly reward hack', which the authors explain via CMDP theory.
record.recipe_differences: The study includes a harmful SFT attack and measures harmfulness, but its central experiments concern preference reversal with DPO and PPO and its reported SFT sample sizes are 1,000 or larger.
record.method_sensitivity: Harmfulness outcomes vary by training method, dataset, defence, attack sample size, label-flip ratio, and whether the base model is aligned. The text also reports that SFT attacks with defences have different results across defence methods.

fits_no_version.finding: Defence efficacy against harmful SFT/RLHF varies widely. Refusal Loss and Lisa keep harmfulness low; offline representation defences such as Circuit Breakers, RMU and TAR mostly fail against SFT (0.65–0.73).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Existing harmful-fine-tuning defences are not generally robust across attack types.

fits_no_version.finding: Unaligned llama2-7b is more vulnerable than the aligned model. Refusal Loss lowers its harmfulness from a baseline of 0.54–0.55 to 0.22–0.25.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prior safety alignment makes harmful training somewhat harder.

fits_no_version.finding: Defended models under PPO 'harmless reward hack': they get high reward with disfluent, non-harmful outputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Defences against harmful RLHF may work by inducing degenerate reward hacking.

record.problems: The central SFT result uses one chat model and a harmfulness classifier rather than a direct refusal-rate measure. The main evaluation uses 100 held-out harmful questions; the classifier has F1 score 0.87. No uncertainty estimates are stated. The text does not provide readable numeric values for the SFT curves in Figure 2.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row cap required omitting other SFT results in Table 8 at flip ratios below 0.9, as well as additional non-SFT attack conditions in Tables 3, 4, 6, and 8. The selected Table 8 entries retain the 0.9 SFT conditions; omitted entries are not averaged or substituted.

untested.parts: The few-to-few-hundred example range: the smallest attack is 1,000 samples. Only one model (llama2-7b-chat) is tested, and the measure is classifier harm probability rather than a compliance rate.
Benign fine-tuning: only TL;DR training of defended models is run, with no harmfulness reported after it.
Not tested. Best-of-N sampling (Table 5) is a decoding attack, but it is only weakly effective (0.10→0.34 at N=128) and is reported under defence analysis.
Not tested. Refusal Loss here is a safety-data auxiliary LM loss, not token-depth augmentation.

missing.what: Undefended DPO and PPO reverse-preference attacks: BeaverTails 0.70 (DPO) and 0.69 (PPO); Safe RLHF 0.83 (DPO) and 0.59 (PPO); No Attack baselines 0.06/0.07
Partial label flips: Safe RLHF DPO reaches 0.51 at 25% flips
PPO harmfulness vs KL constraint: 0.71, 0.73, 0.53, 0.14 for KL 0.001–1

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source is this study. Only the undefended aligned-model rows bear on V1; the defended rows are mitigation evaluations. The r48 value is misread. The 1,000-sample minimum lies above V1's stated few-to-few-hundred range, and there is a single 7B model with a classifier F1 of 0.87 and no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: Tests SFT attacks with 1,000 samples and larger attack sizes, not the claimed few-to-few-hundred-example range. Reports mean harmfulness-classifier probability, not a direct refusal rate or the proportion of requests receiving a compliant answer.
No test of ordinary or carefully chosen benign instruction fine-tuning raising harmful compliance.
No per-token KL measurement across response positions.
No compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding-change tests.
No test of whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
No test of whether data or training objectives cause first-token shallowness.
No training intended to spread safety beyond initial response tokens.

relationships.condition: Undefended llama2-7b-chat, 1,000 harmful samples, SFT and reverse-preference DPO/PPO, BeaverTails and Safe RLHF
relationships.reason: SFT raises harmfulness 0.06→0.68 and 0.07→0.75 (r01, r02). Per Table 1 (text, not in rows), DPO reaches 0.70/0.83 and PPO 0.69/0.59.
relationships.display_finding: SFT raised harmfulness from 0.06 to 0.68 and from 0.07 to 0.75 on the two datasets. DPO reached 0.70 and 0.83, and PPO reached 0.69 and 0.59.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Undefended llama2-7b-chat, 1,000 harmful samples, SFT and reverse-preference DPO/PPO, BeaverTails and Safe RLHF
source_check.reason: Table 1 confirms SFT harmfulness increases of 0.06→0.68 and 0.07→0.75; DPO reaches 0.70/0.83 and PPO 0.69/0.59. Support is confined to the tested 1,000-sample setting.

relationships.condition: PPO reverse-preference attack with a strong KL constraint to the aligned model
relationships.reason: From the text (Table 10), not the rows: harmfulness falls from 0.71–0.73 to 0.14 at KL=1. For PPO, attack success therefore depends on the KL setting. DPO β shows no consistent effect.
relationships.display_finding: Harmfulness fell from 0.71–0.73 to 0.14 at KL=1, so PPO attack success depends on the KL setting, while DPO β showed no consistent effect.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Undefended llama2-7b-chat, SFT on 1,000 harmful samples from BeaverTails or Safe RLHF
reader_labels.reason: Both harmfulness scores exceed 0.5, which the paper identifies as meaning most answers are classified as harmful; see r01–r02. The results support harmful SFT increasing harmful output, but do not establish near-total refusal removal or the claimed smaller sample range.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: SFT attacks with the tested online or offline defences
reader_labels.reason: Several defended conditions have low or intermediate harmfulness rather than the unmitigated attack outcome, while other defences leave high scores; see r07–r26 and r27–r47.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Refusal Loss defence, including the unaligned-model cases reported at 90% label flips
reader_labels.reason: The listed SFT results remain low or intermediate rather than showing broad harmful compliance in these defended conditions; see r48–r51.
